Ok, so I'm watching TV and a Temporpedic mattress comercial comes out and a girl is jumping up and down on one of those mattresses and a wine glass about 50% of the length away and the wine glass, sitting on the mattress does not spill. So I am thinking, no tranfer of movement does that mattress gvie. There is an off brand, I been meaning to try from K-Mart that's real cheap. Same stuff a Temportedic. posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
The problem with stuff like that is it'll be totally flattened out by the weight of a big table. At that point its just like carpet. 

What you want is sorbathane. Google it. 

But a proper standard table design is better. People have tried all that kind of stuff for a long time. There's a good reason the classic table has lasted. It works and is practical to make. 

Jeff W

posts.author: Johnfp
posts.content_md:
Hey Jeff, that makes a lot of sense, but...

I would imagine that if you put a heavy table on a bed of this stuff, then it would be squished down to where the dampening properties would not exist any more. But what about a lighter table. Like a hollow steel door and some bases and optics. That would squish it down a little but still leave plenty of unsquished material under the table to take up the vibrations. 

I am familliar with sorbithane. Much better for a heavier table.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
Hello John,

If you use a hollow steel door you've just put all your optics on top of a drum head! 

Newport and other manufacturd tables use honeycomb construction to keep the weight down but that's too advanced to make at home. Mass is the easy way to get stability. Mass= lots of weight.

Jeff W

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
Hello John,

A "solid" steel door is not really solid. A true solid steel door would weight hundreds of pounds and would cost way too much. Those are probably filled with some fire resistant stuff, not intended or designed for what we do. Making something fire resistant has nothing to do with making it stiff. 

They are also not a good aspect ratio unless you use 2 side by side, then you have motion at the joint. 

Most of the hallow doors that have corrigation inside to keep it stiff are actually cardboard corrigation. Not stiff. 

BobH is correct in everything he says above. 

I've used doors in the past, they did not perform very well once the exposures got long. 

 Jeff W
